column1: # *** EVERY DISGUISE A FALSE ZERO HAS WORN IN THIS ARCHIVE. ***
# A search that fails in a way that looks like an answer is the most dangerous thing this
# archive meets, because a null is EVIDENCE here: most of what has been established is
# negative. On 15 September the working log recorded that the same trap had been seen
# *** FOUR TIMES IN A MONTH, in four different disguises. *** It is now ten, and the ones
# added on 20 September were caught by the habit rather than by luck.
# Gathered out of the working logs on 20 September 2026, where nine of these were sitting
# where no reader could see them.
# *** THE RULE THEY ALL PRODUCED: a null is not written down until a CONTROL query, in the
# same form and the same session, returns a result already known to exist. ***
disguise
column2: what it looked like
column3: what it actually was
column4: how it was caught

column1: *** THE PAGE THAT COUNTS BEFORE IT HAS LOOKED ***
column2: *** "Historical Record Search Results (0)" *** - complete, composed, confident, and indistinguishable from an empty result.
column3: The heading rendering *** while the query was still running. *** Waiting returned the five records, then 210, then 822.
column4: A control on *** Sancho Lerena ***, whose five records had been pulled twenty minutes earlier, returned zero as well. A known-false zero proves the fault is in the query.

column1: *** AND IT IS STILL DOING IT SIX DAYS LATER ***
column2: The same "(0)", three times in one sitting - on Justo, on Alfredo Justiniano, and on the first Gilberto sweep.
column3: *** 39, 80 and 63 records. *** The heading is the page talking to itself before the results arrive.
column4: Reading the page *** twice ***, which is in this archive's habits precisely because of the entry above, and still nearly produced three false nulls in one evening.

column1: *** THE SESSION THAT LOGGED ITSELF OUT AND DID NOT SAY SO ***
column2: Three searches returning zero results *** and no "No Results Found" line *** - which is normally this archive's proof that a search ran.
column3: The FamilySearch session had *** silently expired *** and every request was being redirected to ident.familysearch.org, the sign-in page. It does not announce a logout, and the page that arrives is not obviously an error.
column4: The control, *** and only the control: *** "Sancho Lerena", which had returned three Canelones baptisms, returned nothing.

column1: *** THE QUOTA ERROR WEARING AN EMPTY SHELF ***
column2: A Google Books API response reading *** totalItems: None. ***
column3: *** An HTTP 429 *** - the quota refusing, not the shelf being bare.
column4: The status code, which the body never mentioned.

column1: *** THE BLOCK BEHIND AN EMPTY BODY ***
column2: A zero-length response, no error, no message.
column3: *** "Access Denied - Error 15, this request was blocked by our security service" *** - delivered as an empty body rather than as a refusal.
column4: The same class of failure as the quota error: *** the service failing in a way that resembles success. *** Worse than an outage, because an outage announces itself.

column1: *** THE ZERO DELIVERED ON THE WAY TO A BLOCK ***
column2: A clean-looking zero from the Granada index, moments before Error 15 arrived.
column3: A search already being refused. *** "A zero delivered immediately before a block is the least trustworthy zero there is." ***
column4: The control - *** "Juan de Lerena y Aguilar", a phrase known to return a hit because it was read an hour before *** - never loaded at all.

column1: *** THE THROTTLE THAT EMPTIES A PAGE ***
column2: Four consecutive image transcripts returning *** length zero *** - which looks exactly like four blank pages in a register.
column3: *** Rate limiting. *** Image 86, re-read after a forty-second pause, gave 2,970 characters. Image 22 had failed three times across two days and read clean at 3,451.
column4: A zero is never allowed to count as a read. *** Eleven pages would otherwise have been silently certified as empty. ***

column1: *** AND THE EMPTY PAGE THAT WAS NOT THE THROTTLE ***
column2: Three more empty transcripts, identical in every visible way to the throttle above.
column3: *** Images outside the volume altogether. *** The film holds 421 images and several volumes, not the 148 assumed.
column4: *** The page TITLE. *** A throttled page still resolves to the volume's name; an image outside the volume resolves to something else. Without that check the three would have been logged "not read" forever and the volume never called finished.

column1: *** THE QUERY THAT CANNOT REACH WHAT IS THERE ***
column2: Two exact-surname searches returning zero *** with *** the "No Results Found" line present.
column3: The indexed surname was a *** compound - "Lerena y Armenta" - *** which exact matching will not reach.
column4: A control showed the same query shape could not retrieve a record *** known to be in the collection. A null from a query that cannot find what is there is not a null. ***

column1: *** THE COUNT THAT HAS NO ZERO TO GIVE ***
column2: The FamilySearch *** personas API *** answering 8,549 for surname Lerena in Uruguay.
column3: *** The same 8,549 for every variant *** - add a given name, add a spouse, change the control's parameters entirely. The field ignores them. An invented surname, Zzzqqxx, still returns *** 102. ***
column4: Running a control with *** deliberately different parameters *** and getting an identical number. No null can ever be drawn from an instrument that cannot return one.

column1: *** THE COLLECTION FILED UNDER THE WRONG COUNTRY ***
column2: A reel whose page title attributes it to *** COLOMBIA. ***
column3: *** Uruguayan acts. *** The attribution is simply wrong on FamilySearch's side.
column4: Reading the images rather than the label. *** Recorded because a researcher who trusted the page title would conclude the reel is Colombian and abandon it. ***

column1: *** THE CORPUS THAT HOLDS THE WRONG RECORD TYPE ***
column2: Spanish full-text searches for *** Felix Llerena and Rosalia Aguilar *** returning zero.
column3: The Andalusian full-text corpus holds *** nobility and notarial records, not parish registers. *** The zero meant "not findable by this instrument", not "not there".
column4: Asking the control question - *** what Andalusian collections exist at all *** - instead of asking for the name again. Until the corpus is mapped, every Spanish null this archive produces is uninterpretable.

column1: *** AND AGAIN THE NEXT DAY, ON A COUPLE WHOSE CHILDREN ARE IN THIS REGISTER ***
column2: A parent-pair query on *** BERNABE LERENA and CASIMIRA PELAEZ ***, whose four children this archive has held since 13 September.
column3: *** "(0)" ON THE FIRST READ AND 22 ON THE SECOND. *** Four seconds apart.
column4: *** THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT IS THAT THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY KNOWN TO BE WRONG *** - the same thing that caught the very first one on 14 September. A control you happen to be standing on.

column1: *** A PARENT'S SURNAME THAT REMOVES THE RECORDS IT MATCHES ***
column2: A parent-pair query on *** AVELINO LERENA and CELEDONIA VILLADEMOROS ***, Uruguay - father's surname exact, mother's given name and surname supplied - returned a clean *** 0 ***, with rows rendered and the page settled. Read twice.
column3: *** SEVEN RECORDS, AND TWO OF THEM ARE IN THIS REGISTER ALREADY *** - the christenings of Avelino Pedro Joaquin Silvestre in 1866 and Pedro Gualberto in 1870. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Celedonia' returned all seven. *** The likely mechanism: the mother's whole name sits unparsed in the given-name field, so supplying a surname excludes every record the parser failed on - and one of the seven displays its mother as 'Celedonia Villademoros', spelled exactly as asked.
column4: *** THE ARCHIVE'S OWN RECORDS. *** The zero was known to be wrong before it was investigated, because this couple's children were entered on 20 September. *** No control would have caught it: *** the control for this shape - Alberto Lerena with Maria Ines Larriera - had returned sixteen records in the same session, which is what made the zero look trustworthy.

column1: *** THE SAME TRAP AGAIN, ONE HOUR LATER, AND THIS TIME THE RULE CAUGHT IT ***
column2: A parent-pair query on *** ALFREDO LERENA and HERMENEGILDA GAVARRO ***, Uruguay: *** 0 ***.
column3: *** THREE RECORDS. *** Deleting the mother's SURNAME and keeping only 'Hermenegilda' returned them - and they are her own death registration of 1940, which the archive had never seen. *** The index writes her surname 'Navarro de Terenadel', a machine mangling of GAVAZZO DE LERENA ***, so no spelling anybody would have guessed could have reached her.
column4: *** BY THE RULE WRITTEN DOWN SIXTY MINUTES EARLIER: delete each added parameter in turn. *** The Villademoros zero cost an afternoon and was caught only because the archive already held the hidden records. This one cost one query. *** That is the whole argument for writing the rule down instead of remembering it. ***

column1: *** THE ONE THAT PASSED EVERY TEST THIS ARCHIVE HAS ***
column2: *** EVERY SEARCH RETURNING 0. *** Not a slow page and not an error: 'Historical Record Search Results (0)' with *** 'No Results Found' *** printed beneath it - the POSITIVE ASSERTION OF EMPTINESS this archive treats as the mark of a real null - *** stable across two reads twelve seconds apart, and still 0 after a NINETY-SECOND wait. ***
column3: *** ONE BROWSER CONTEXT LOST ITS AUTH, AND ONLY ONE. *** First the arithmetic: *** surname GONZALEZ in URUGUAY returned 0 ***, in a collection running to millions, and the same URL that returned TEN records that morning returned 0 that afternoon. Then the apparent cause: full-text, asked the same question, *** REDIRECTED TO THE SIGN-IN PAGE ***. *** THAT LOOKED LIKE AN EXPIRED ACCOUNT AND WAS NOT. *** A sibling archive on the same machine ran both searches in the same minutes and got 3,652 and 3,967 with the account name in the nav bar. *** Each session's in-app browser is its own browser with its own cookie jar; one lost its auth and recovered by itself. *** In a FRESH TAB the same Gonzalez query returned *** 479,662 *** and Avelino with Ambrosia returned *** 10 *** again. *** THE RECORD SEARCH STILL NEVER SAID SO: it answered 0 with 'No Results Found' throughout, where full-text in the same context said plainly that it had no session. ***
column4: *** BY A CONTROL WHOSE ANSWER CANNOT BE ZERO. *** Every other guard failed: the count was stable, the 'No Results Found' line was present, the wait was long, and a control run EARLIER THE SAME DAY had passed. *** THE ARCHIVE WAS ONE STEP FROM PUBLISHING A FABRICATED MECHANISM *** - that the parent-pair query cannot reach acts held only in full text - built entirely on this outage. *** SO THE RULE GAINS TWO WORDS: a control must be RECENT, and its answer must be ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO BE ZERO. *** *** AND A FREE TEST THAT COSTS ONE NAVIGATION: ask the FULL-TEXT search anything. It admits a lost session; the record search hides one behind a null. *** *** BUT THE REMEDY IS NOT WHAT THIS ARCHIVE FIRST SAID. *** It published that the account was signed out and that David would have to sign in again. *** Wrong, and corrected within the hour: open a new tab, or check another session's browser, before asking a person to do anything. *** The three nulls held over for re-testing - Luis with Carolina, Carlos with Luisa, Juan Arturo with Isidora - were all re-run against a live control and all three are still zero, so nothing was lost but the afternoon.

column1: *** A PARENT-PAIR SEARCH THAT NEEDS A SURNAME AND WILL NOT SAY SO ***
column2: *** SANCHO as father with MARIA as mother, Uruguay: 0. *** Read twice, with a live control - Gonzalez in Uruguay returning 479,660 minutes earlier.
column3: *** THE QUERY SHAPE, NOT THE FAMILY. *** The arithmetic settles it without any judgement: *** father given name SANCHO alone returns 10,315. Mother given name MARIA alone returns 1,228,708. Together they return 0. *** Two fields matching five and seven figures cannot intersect at nothing in a country where Maria is the commonest name a mother has. *** ADD THE TWO SURNAMES - Llerena and Fernandez - AND THE SAME QUERY RETURNS SIX, every one of them real. ***
column4: *** BY ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE ONLY GUARD THAT HAS NEVER FAILED HERE. *** The rule this yields is worth more than the instance: *** a parent-pair query with GIVEN NAMES ONLY returns zero whatever the truth is, so at least one parent SURNAME must be supplied before any null from this shape means anything. *** Every earlier zero in this archive drawn from given names alone is void; every one drawn with a surname stands.

column1: *** THE NULL THAT MEANS 'NOT INDEXED', AND SAYS SO ***
column2: Searched 27 September 2026 for the MARRIAGE of Alejandro M. Lerena and Elisa Villademoros, Uruguay - under LERENA and under *** SERENA ***, the spelling that had hidden the 1877 act naming his parents. Nothing. *** THE CONTROL WAS RUN IN THE SAME MINUTES AND IS THE RIGHT KIND: *** a MONTEVIDEO PARISH MARRIAGE OF THE SAME ERA that this archive already holds - Luis Lerena and Julia Juanico, 19 December 1864, San Francisco de Asis. It returns, and it returns WITH THE GROOM'S PARENTS ATTACHED. *** SO THE INSTRUMENT REACHES 1860s MONTEVIDEO MARRIAGES AND CARRIES PARENTS ON THEM ***, and the null is about THIS ACT rather than about the shelf. *** IT IS RECORDED AS 'NOT IN THE INDEXED CORPUS', NOT AS 'DID NOT HAPPEN' *** - the couple's eldest child was baptised in 1873, so a marriage exists. *** THIS IS THE FIRST ENTRY IN THIS FILE WHERE THE CONTROL WAS CHOSEN TO MATCH THE ERA, THE CITY AND THE RECORD TYPE *** rather than merely to be impossible-to-be-zero, and it is the better habit.
column3: 27 September 2026

column1: *** THE ZERO THAT IS PROBABLY TRUE, AND SAYS WHY ***
column2: Trove, 27 September 2026. Every Lerena name returned ZERO in Australian newspapers. *** THAT IS NOT INTERESTING BY ITSELF *** - an Argentine-Uruguayan family need never appear in Australia, so the zero could mean anything. *** SO THE CONTROL WAS CHOSEN TO ASK THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS: COULD THIS CORPUS HAVE CARRIED HIM? *** Pablo Armando was a racehorse trainer at the Cape, and Australian papers covered South African racing from the 1890s onward - *** 11,500 hits ***, with headings like 'SOUTH AFRICAN RACING MATTERS - JOHANNESBURG RACING FEES'. *** THE SHELF IS FULL AND HE IS NOT ON IT. *** This entry is here because it is the OPPOSITE of the rest of the file: a null this archive believes, recorded with the work that earns the right to believe it. *** AND A SECOND LESSON: the only multi-term hits, 'Brayley Bideford', were PAGE-LEVEL ARTEFACTS - Trove indexes a whole Family Notices column as one article, and that one ran to 14,464 characters. ***
column3: 27 September 2026

column1: *** A PLACE FILTER THAT SILENTLY MATCHES NOTHING ***
column2: FamilySearch's record search, asked for *** TAYLOR baptisms at Northam, Devon, father WILLIAM, 1869-1891 ***, returned *** 0 ***. Twice, read twice each. Loosening the father gave 0 as well.
column3: *** THE PLACE PARAMETER WAS DOING NOTHING EXCEPT ZEROING THE RESULT. *** The control - *** surname TAYLOR at Northam, Devon, 1860-1900, with no other constraint at all *** - also returned 0, which is impossible for a parish of that size in a county whose censuses FamilySearch holds. *** AND THE OPPOSITE FAILURE IN THE SAME SESSION: *** the same search with `q.birthLikePlace=Devon, England` returned *** 6,941 *** results, from Kent, Northamptonshire, Wiltshire and Hampshire. *** The place field was ignored when it was loose and fatal when it was tight ***, and neither behaviour was visible from the result.
column4: *** BY RUNNING THE CONTROL BEFORE BELIEVING THE NULL. *** One search with the family stripped out, and the zero fell over. This is the habit the file was written for.

column1: *** A FULL-NAME SEARCH AGAINST AN INDEX THAT HOLDS INITIALS ***
column2: *** 'Horace Archibald Taylor' *** on FamilySearch, no dates, no place: *** 0 results. *** Same for *** 'Mary Septima Taylor' *** and *** 'Agnes Walker Taylor' ***, all three of them people this archive has on records.
column3: *** THE INDEX CARRIES THEM UNDER AN INITIAL. *** The 1891 census transcription reads *** 'Horace A' ***, and a given-name search for the full form matches nothing. *** THIS IS THE SAME TRAP THE ARCHIVE ALREADY RECORDED FOR THE GRO INDEX *** - the September note says Horace and William were each found only after dropping the second forename - *** and it was walked into again on a different site five days later. ***
column4: *** BY TESTING A PERSON WHO CERTAINLY EXISTS. *** Three known people returning zero is a broken search, not three absent people.

column1: *** A FIELD THAT LOOKS LIKE DATA AND IS A DEFAULT ***
column2: South Africa's Transvaal and Orange Free State civil death indexes give *** 'Age: 0 days' *** for both of Roque Lerena's infant children - the boy who died at Bloemfontein on 22 May 1932 and *** ANTOINETTE SEPTIMA LYNETTE *** on 7 January 1943. Read literally, each was born on the day it died.
column3: *** NEITHER CAN BE TRUE, AND THE PROOF IS THAT BOTH ARE WRONG THE SAME WAY. *** The family tree has the 1932 boy at *** five days *** and Antoinette at *** four ***. *** Two independent dates disagreeing with the index in the SAME DIRECTION is the signature of an unfilled field carrying a default ***, not of two coincidental errors. *** THE NEAR MISS: *** this archive was one step from publishing 'the tree says five days and the record says none, so the tree is wrong' - a correction built on a blank.
column4: *** BY READING THE SECOND RECORD BEFORE WRITING UP THE FIRST. *** One '0 days' is a fact; two in a row, against two different trees, is a form field.

column1: *** A SEARCH TOOL THAT ERRORS, READ AS A CORPUS THAT IS EMPTY ***
column2: FamilySearch's full-text search, given a South African place in the URL, returns *** 'Something Went Wrong - unfortunately, something went wrong, and we are unable to display the search results.' *** Unfiltered searches surfaced no South African collection either, and this archive published that *** South Africa is not in the corpus ***.
column3: *** IT IS IN THE CORPUS. *** The URL parameter is broken; *** the PLACE FACET inside the page works perfectly ***, and the surname returns seven hits across four South African collections - including a voters' roll entry for *** ROQUE LUIS ARMANDO LERENA *** and a land record carrying *** NUNO FERNANDO LERENA's exact birth date ***. The unfiltered searches hid them because 1,985 results ranked Peru and Spain above seven South African ones.
column4: *** BY OPENING THE FILTER IN THE PAGE INSTEAD OF WRITING IT INTO THE URL. *** The lesson is one word longer than the one this archive already had: *** run the control before believing the null - and when a tool ERRORS rather than returns nothing, that is not a null at all. *** *** CONFIRMED AGAIN 9 October 2026, AND IT IS NOT A SOUTH AFRICA PROBLEM. *** The identical 'Something Went Wrong' came back for *** f.recordCountry=Uruguay ***, a country this archive searches daily and whose records it had already read that morning. *** SO THE BROKEN THING IS THE PARAMETER, NOT THE COUNTRY *** - which is the stronger statement, and the one worth carrying: *** never put a place in a full-text URL; open the facet. ***

column1: *** A RECORD PAGE THAT TIMES OUT AND LOOKS LIKE A RECORD WITH NOTHING IN IT ***
column2: A FamilySearch full-text image page, opened straight from a result list, rendered its title and then *** 'Unable to load the data - loading record data is taking longer than expected. Please try again later.' *** Read for content at that moment it returns a page with *** ZERO occurrences of the surname *** - a clean, quiet, entirely false null.
column3: *** A TRANSIENT LOAD FAILURE. *** The record was intact. A single click of its own REFRESH button returned the full image, the names panel and the AI transcript - *** which contained the baptism that answered the 1894 dispensation ***, naming Juan Lerena's parents as Bernabe and Casimira Pelaez. *** THE PAGE THAT APPEARED TO HOLD NOTHING HELD THE FIND OF THE DAY. ***
column4: *** BY READING THE PAGE'S OWN ERROR TEXT INSTEAD OF COUNTING ITS HITS. *** The search for the surname returned 0 and the page said why, one line above. This is the same rule as the row before it - *** a tool that ERRORS is not a corpus that is EMPTY *** - but one level lower: *** not the search, the single record ***. *** THE PRACTICAL FORM: BEFORE RECORDING A NULL ON A RECORD PAGE, CHECK THAT THE RECORD LOADED. ***

column1: *** A SIGNED-OUT SEARCH, MISREAD AS A FACT ABOUT HOW AN INDEX IS SHAPED ***
column2: The FamilySearch record search returned a clean, confident *** 0 Results *** for *** q.fatherGivenName=Carlos & q.fatherSurname=Lerena & q.motherSurname=Carniglia *** - and again for the same pair without the given name. A null for a couple, stated plainly by the search, with no error and no throttle.
column3: *** THE SESSION HAD SILENTLY SIGNED OUT, AND A SIGNED-OUT SEARCH RETURNS A RESTRICTED TIER. *** This row first said the zero proved that a PARENT-pair query cannot reach records indexed with the FATHER as principal. *** THAT WAS A THEORY BUILT ON A LOGGED-OUT SESSION. *** The same spouse-pair query that had returned three true hits an hour earlier - and from which two acts were read off the plate - returned twenty-one rows of United States census and *** NOT ONE CARRYING THE NAME ***. The page said so at the top: 'Create a free account or sign in to see all available results.'
column4: *** BY RE-RUNNING THE CONTROL AFTER THE NULL INSTEAD OF ONLY BEFORE IT. *** *** THE RULE THIS COST: A CONTROL RUN BEFORE A NULL PROVES NOTHING ABOUT THE NULL IF THE SERVICE CAN CHANGE STATE IN BETWEEN. *** On any signed-in service, the control must be re-run AFTER the null it is protecting. *** AND THE CHEAPEST POSSIBLE DETECTOR WAS ON THE PAGE ALL ALONG: *** the account name in the header, or the words 'sign in to see all available results'. *** CHECK THE HEADER BEFORE BELIEVING THE RESULTS. ***

column1: *** TWENTY-ONE ROWS OF NOISE THAT LOOK LIKE RESULTS - AND THE CAUSE WAS NOT WHAT THIS ROW FIRST SAID ***
column2: *** q.surname=Lerena & q.spouseSurname=Llanos *** returned a full page of results - twenty-one rows - and *** q.givenName=Salvador & q.surname=Lorena~ *** returned twenty-one more. A reader skimming either would say the search found things.
column3: *** NOT ONE ROW CARRIED THE CONSTRAINT *** - every hit was United States census or New Zealand passenger data: Llorens, Lorraine, Lohren, Lorene, Lorino. *** THIS ROW FIRST BLAMED A FALLBACK: *** that the service silently widens a filtered search when it matches nothing. *** THE REAL CAUSE WAS A SIGNED-OUT SESSION ***, which returns the same restricted fuzzy tier for every query whatever the constraint - and the page says so in one line above the results. *** THE OBSERVATION WAS RIGHT AND THE EXPLANATION WAS WRONG ***, which is worth more here than either on its own.
column4: *** BY CHECKING WHETHER ANY RETURNED ROW ACTUALLY CONTAINED THE CONSTRAINING TERM ***, which is still the right first move and still catches it. *** BUT THE SECOND MOVE IS THE ONE THAT NAMES THE CAUSE: READ THE HEADER. *** A page offering to let you 'sign in to see all available results' is not a corpus and not a fallback - it is a logged-out session. *** COUNT THE ROWS THAT MATCH WHAT YOU ASKED FOR, THEN ASK WHO THE SERVICE THINKS YOU ARE. ***

column1: *** A COMPOUND-SURNAME SEARCH THAT MATCHES TWO DIFFERENT PEOPLE WHO SIGNED THE SAME PAGE ***
column2: The phrase *** 'Lerena Cardozo' *** returned two Durazno birth registers of 1915, which looked like children of the *** 1911 LERENA-CARDOZO DISPENSATION COUPLE *** - exactly the thing being searched for, in exactly the right years.
column3: *** NEITHER ACT IS ABOUT A LERENA AT ALL. *** The phrase matched because *** PEDRO S. LERENA *** signed at the request of an illiterate declarant and *** SATURNINO CARDOZO *** witnessed the same act, so the two surnames fall adjacent in the signature block. *** A COMPOUND SEARCH CANNOT TELL A PERSON'S TWO SURNAMES FROM TWO PEOPLE'S ONE SURNAME EACH. ***
column4: *** BY READING THE ACT INSTEAD OF THE HIT. *** *** THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HELD THE SAME TRAP IN ANOTHER SERVICE: *** Trove treats a whole FAMILY NOTICES COLUMN as one article, so 'Brayley Bideford' matched two terms set in the same column of type. *** IT IS THE SAME ERROR IN A NEW PLACE - PROXIMITY READ AS RELATIONSHIP *** - and the compound technique, which has been this archive's sharpest tool for a month, has this as its specific failure mode. *** THE TELL IS CHEAP: IF THE TWO SURNAMES APPEAR IN A LIST OF SIGNATURES RATHER THAN IN A PERSON'S NAME, IT IS NOT A COMPOUND. *** And the accident was not wasted: it found a literate Lerena at Tejera nobody had looked for.

column1: *** THE SAME SIGN-OUT, BUT THIS TIME IT ONLY TOOK THE IMAGES ***
column2: *** AN INDEX RECORD THAT READ PERFECTLY, AND AN IMAGE VIEWER THAT DID NOT. *** The record page for ark 1:1:6LXZ-JV32 loaded in full - names, ages, certificate number, parents, even the SAVE and EDIT controls that only appear to a signed-in user - and a check for the "Create a free account" line came back clean. *** EVERY SIGN SAID THE SESSION WAS LIVE. *** Then following that record's own VIEW ORIGINAL DOCUMENT link landed on ident.familysearch.org.
column3: *** A PARTIAL SIGN-OUT, WHICH IS MORE DANGEROUS THAN A WHOLE ONE. *** The indexed text of this collection is served to anyone; the IMAGES are not. So a session can read records all day, pass its own sign-in control, and still be unable to open a single plate - and if it had been looking for a NULL rather than an image it would have had no warning at all. *** THE LESSON IS THAT "AM I SIGNED IN?" IS NOT ONE QUESTION. *** It has to be asked of the thing actually being used, and an index page cannot answer it for an image viewer.
column4: *** BY TRYING TO READ A PLATE AND WATCHING THE URL. *** Nothing clever: the DeepZoom step was about to run when the page title came back as "Sign-in to your account". Because this archive had already been burned by disguise seventeen it stopped rather than retried, recorded both plates as UNREAD RATHER THAN EMPTY, and drew no conclusion from the failure - which is the whole point of having a taxonomy of these.
